name: A Culture Orbital
blurb: A ring three million kilometres across, spun for gravity, with engineered weather and no laws, money, work or death. Ask the Mind politely and it will build you a continent.

name: Aboard the Nautilus
blurb: A submarine with a pipe organ, a library of twelve thousand volumes and a captain who has renounced the surface entirely. Meals are exclusively from the sea.

name: Ahch-To
blurb: A green island of stone huts and impossible steps in a cold ocean, the first Jedi temple, and thousands of very confident seabirds.

name: Airstrip One
blurb: London as a province of Oceania: rationed, bombed, watched from every wall, and at war with a power whose identity has always been the one it is at war with now.
about: Orwell wrote it on Jura while dying of tuberculosis, and set it in a Britain of post-war shortages he had actually lived through — the gin is bad, the razor blades have run out, the lift doesn't work. The Ministry of Truth rewrites yesterday's papers daily; Newspeak is designed so that certain thoughts become unsayable and therefore unthinkable. Almost every English word for surveillance now comes from this book.

name: Ankh-Morpork
blurb: The Discworld's great, filthy, thriving city, built on the silt of a river too thick to drink and too thin to plough. Run by a tyrant who is very good at it, and by guilds for everything including thieves.
about: A million people, several dozen species and one Patrician. The Guild of Thieves is licensed and issues receipts; the Watch has grown from three drunks to a functioning police force; the Post Office works again. Pratchett used it to write about every civic institution in turn — the mint, the newspaper, the railway, the opera house — which is why the city changes measurably from book to book. Nothing in it is safe and everything in it is funny.

name: Arrakis
blurb: The only source of the spice, and the harshest inhabited world known. Water is currency, worms are three hundred metres long, and the Fremen do not need your help.

name: Asgard
blurb: A golden city on a floating disc at the end of a rainbow bridge, full of immortals who consider a thousand years a reasonable length of time to hold a grudge.
about: Norse myth reworked by Kirby into something closer to space opera — the Aesir are aliens, the Bifrost is a transit system, and Odin's throne room is drawn like a cathedral built by someone who has never heard of restraint. Heimdall stands at the bridge and sees everything in all nine realms, which makes him both the setting's best character and its biggest plot problem. Ragnarök is not avoidable; it is scheduled.

name: Atlantis
blurb: Concentric rings of land and water, walls sheathed in orichalcum, and an empire that grew arrogant and was swallowed in a single day and night.

name: Beyond the Wall
blurb: Free Folk, giants, mammoths and something much worse coming south. Genuinely unspoilt. Genuinely will kill you.

name: Braavos
blurb: A city of canals in a lagoon, founded by escaped slaves, run by banks, and guarded by a colossus. Superb food, water-dancing, and a temple you should not visit twice.

name: Bree
blurb: A crossroads town where Men and Hobbits drink in the same room and everyone notices strangers. The Prancing Pony does a good pint and a poor job of keeping secrets.

name: Brobdingnag
blurb: A land of giants where the wasps are the size of partridges and a fall from a table is fatal. The king considers our species a pernicious little race of vermin, and he has a point.

name: Cair Paravel
blurb: The seat of Narnia's kings and queens, on a headland above the eastern sea, with four thrones that stay empty until the right four people arrive.
about: The castle stands where the Great River meets the ocean, and by the later books it is a ruin on an island, because Narnian time runs at a speed nobody in England can predict. Its throne room is the point of the whole country: Narnia is repeatedly saved by children who are told, and eventually believe, that they were always meant to be royalty. Feasts here are described at length and are the best argument for going.

name: Caladan
blurb: A green ocean world of rain, cliffs and fishing fleets — the Atreides homeworld, and everything Arrakis is not. Leaving it was the mistake.

name: Camelot
blurb: One brief shining moment of a castle, a round table with no head, and a kingdom that runs on oaths. It ends badly. Everyone knows it ends badly.

name: Candlekeep
blurb: A fortress library on a crag above the sea, holding every book worth keeping. The entry fee is one book they do not already have, and they usually already have it.
about: The monks of the Binder keep the largest collection in Faerûn, and the admission price — a written work of genuine value — is the most elegant gate in fantasy. You get a month inside. Nobody may remove a book, copy is permitted, and the wards are unpleasant about theft. Baldur's Gate opens here, which means an entire generation's first D&D memory is a library.

name: Casterly Rock
blurb: A castle carved into a mountain above a gold mine that has never run dry. Three times the height of the Wall, and every inch of it paid for.

name: Charn
blurb: A vast dead city under a swollen red sun, where a queen spoke one word and every living thing but herself stopped. There is a bell in the hall, and a sign inviting you to ring it.
about: Lewis's coldest invention: an entire world killed by a single act of spite, preserved as an empty museum of its own greatness. The temptation of the bell — a hand-lettered verse daring the reader to strike it — is one of children's literature's best traps, because you already know the child will, and so would you. Jadis leaves Charn and becomes the White Witch of Narnia.

name: Cimmeria
blurb: A grey land of cloud, crag and gloom that produces nothing but iron-hard people and a marked disinclination to stay in it. Conan left as soon as he could.
about: Howard wrote a poem about Cimmeria before he wrote a story set there, and the poem is better: 'a gloomy land that seems to hold all winds and clouds and dreams'. The Cimmerians are barbarians in the technical sense — no cities, no writing, no kings — and Howard's whole argument is that this makes them more honest than the civilisations they raid. The gods here are not worth praying to and everybody knows it.

name: Cittàgazze
blurb: A warm Mediterranean city of cafés and shuttered palazzi, entirely empty of adults. The Spectres ate them. The children are fine, until they aren't.
about: The city of magpies sits at a crossroads between worlds, which is why so many windows open onto it. Its people made the subtle knife, cut too many holes, and let the Spectres in — creatures that consume adult consciousness and leave the body standing. Children can't see them and are ignored by them, so Cittàgazze is a beautiful abandoned resort run by feral teenagers. Pullman's most effective horror image, achieved with no gore at all.

name: Cloud City, Bespin
blurb: A tibanna-gas mining platform floating in the habitable band of a gas giant. Superb sunsets, excellent dining, and the hospitality has a poor historical record.

name: Coruscant
blurb: A single city covering an entire planet, a thousand levels deep. The upper levels have opera and senators; the lower levels have everything else.
photoTopics: Hong Kong dense high rise night

name: Dagobah
blurb: A swamp planet with no cities, no technology and a very strong presence in the Force. One resident, who is not accepting visitors.

name: Death's Domain
blurb: A black garden with black flowers and a very large house, kept by an anthropomorphic personification who is trying hard to understand people and getting closer than most people manage.
about: Death built it himself, working from descriptions, which is why the perspective is slightly wrong everywhere and the fish in the pond are made of bone. He keeps a white horse called Binky, an adopted daughter, a granddaughter and an increasingly complicated interest in humanity. He is not cruel. He is simply the last thing you see, and he takes the job seriously. THERE IS NO JUSTICE. THERE IS JUST ME.

name: Deep Space Nine & Bajor
blurb: A recovering world of terraced farms and monasteries, and the Cardassian station above it beside a stable wormhole. The best bar in the quadrant, run by the least trustworthy man in it.

name: Diagon Alley
blurb: A crooked shopping street reached by tapping the right brick behind a Charing Cross Road pub. Wands, owls, cauldrons, and a bank staffed by goblins who do not care for you.
about: The best single piece of world-building in the books: an entire economy rendered as a shopping trip, with prices, brand names and a queue. Gringotts runs on carts and dragons; Ollivanders has been making wands since 382 BC and the wand chooses the wizard. Knockturn Alley branches off it and is where the plot goes when it needs to get unpleasant.

name: District 12
blurb: A coal-mining district at the edge of the map, fenced off, half-starved and largely ignored — which turns out to be the only useful thing about it.
about: The Seam, the Hob black market, the woods beyond an electric fence that is usually switched off for want of power. Collins based it on Appalachian mining towns, and the detail that matters is that hunting outside the fence is illegal but tolerated, because the Peacekeepers also want to eat. The bakery, the meadow and the mockingjays all pay off later, which is why the place is worth walking around.

name: Dorne
blurb: Sun, blood oranges and water gardens, run by the only kingdom the dragons never conquered. Relaxed about most things, unforgiving about the rest.

name: Dragonstone
blurb: A black volcanic island carved with dragons, sitting on a mountain of dragonglass. Bleak, dramatic, and the ancestral seat of people who marry their siblings.

name: Edoras & Rohan
blurb: A golden hall on a lone hill above endless grass, and the best horses in the world. Come for the riding, stay because someone has taken your horse.

name: Erebor
blurb: The Lonely Mountain — a dwarf kingdom of vaulted halls and a treasury that has caused two wars. Superb metalwork, excellent ale, occasional dragon.

name: Fangorn Forest
blurb: The oldest forest left standing, and it is watching you. Nothing here is in a hurry, including any conversation you may be invited into.

name: Gallifrey
blurb: Orange skies, silver-leaved trees and a glass-domed Citadel of Time Lords who watch everything and interfere with nothing, allegedly. Twin suns rise in the south.

name: Giedi Prime
blurb: A stripped industrial world under a black sun, seat of House Harkonnen. The architecture is brutal, the entertainments are worse, and there is no natural light anywhere.

name: Gont
blurb: A single mountain rising out of the sea, known for goats, goatherds, pirates and wizards. Ged was born on it, and came back to it when everything else was finished.
about: Le Guin opens the first book with Gont and closes the cycle there, which tells you what she thought mattered. The island is poor, steep and cold, and its people are famously taciturn. The mountain is high enough that the villages on its flanks are above the weather; Ogion the Silent walked its paths for years and taught by not speaking, which is the best lesson in the book.

name: Gormenghast
blurb: A castle so vast that whole wings have been forgotten, governed entirely by ritual that nobody understands and nobody may alter. Extraordinary. Suffocating.

name: Helium, Barsoom
blurb: Twin cities of scarlet and yellow towers above the ochre moss of a dying Mars, with flying ships, four-armed green warriors and a princess who needs no rescuing.

name: Helm's Deep
blurb: A fortress wedged into a ravine that has never fallen while men defended it. Spectacular walls, dramatic acoustics, and a strong chance of being asked to hold a line.

name: Highgarden
blurb: Terraced gardens, orchards and the richest farmland in the Seven Kingdoms. The food is the best in the world and so is the poisoning.

name: Hogsmeade
blurb: Britain's only entirely wizarding village: thatched cottages under snow, butterbeer at the Three Broomsticks, and a pub down the road that nobody sensible drinks in.
about: Third-years and above may visit on scheduled weekends, which makes it the closest thing the books have to a holiday destination. Honeydukes has a secret passage in its cellar; the Shrieking Shack is the most haunted building in Britain and is not haunted at all. Butterbeer, invented for the page and later made real by a theme park, is somewhere between cream soda and a hot toddy.

name: Hogwarts
blurb: A thousand-year-old castle of moving staircases, portraits with opinions and a lake with a squid in it. Muggles see a ruin with warning signs. Term begins on 1 September.
about: Four founders, four houses, and a building that actively resists mapping — 142 staircases, some of which go somewhere different on Fridays. The teaching is uneven, the safety record is appalling and the food is superb. The Room of Requirement appears only when you need it; the Forbidden Forest is forbidden for good reasons that nobody enforces. Filming used Alnwick Castle, Durham and Gloucester Cathedrals and Glenfinnan Viaduct, all of which you can actually visit.

name: Holy Terra
blurb: A planet-wide hive city built over the bones of Earth, centred on a golden throne that consumes a thousand psykers a day. Pilgrimage of a lifetime; do not look up.

name: Hoth
blurb: An ice planet with nothing to recommend it except that nobody looks for you here. Night temperatures will kill an unprotected human in minutes.

name: Hyrule
blurb: Green fields and a ruined castle in the middle distance, with a shrine on every horizon and something worth climbing behind it. Bring a paraglider and a great many apples.
about: Hyrule is rebuilt from scratch almost every game — the same kingdom, the same princess, the same sword, a different map. Breath of the Wild's version put the whole thing on one continuous terrain with no loading and a rule that anything you can see, you can walk to, which is the clearest statement of intent in the medium. Miyamoto has said the original came from remembering exploring hillsides and caves as a boy near Kyoto.

name: Isla Nublar
blurb: A tropical island theme park stocked with de-extincted dinosaurs and a security system with a single point of failure. Spared no expense. Should have spared some.

name: Jakku
blurb: A junkyard planet where a fleet came to die. Scavenging is the entire economy and portions are paid in something that expands into bread.

name: Kaer Morhen
blurb: A half-ruined fortress up a mountain trail nobody maintains, where witchers are made and, in winter, where the last handful of them come home to drink and repair their swords.
about: The Trial of the Grasses killed most of the boys put through it and can no longer be performed, because the keep was sacked and the mutagens destroyed — which means the witchers are a profession with no new entrants and a known end date. That elegiac note is the whole series in one building. The winter sequences here, with four monster hunters cooking badly and arguing, are the warmest thing Sapkowski wrote.

name: Kashyyyk
blurb: Wroshyr trees kilometres tall with cities built in the canopy, and a warrior culture of very large people who take debts extremely seriously.

name: King's Landing
blurb: A million people, a Red Keep, and a smell you never fully stop noticing. The politics are magnificent and the life expectancy of anyone interesting is short.

name: Laputa
blurb: A flying island of mathematicians and musicians so lost in abstraction they need servants to flap their ears when it is their turn to speak. The view is remarkable. The conversation is not.

name: Lilliput
blurb: An island empire of people six inches high, currently at war with Blefuscu over which end of an egg to open. Charming for an afternoon; the politics are exhausting.

name: Lothlórien
blurb: Golden mallorn woods where time runs differently and everyone speaks in a way that makes you feel underdressed. You will leave with gifts and an unresolved feeling.

name: Lyra's Oxford
blurb: Oxford as it is in a world with airships, anbaric light and everyone's soul walking beside them as an animal. Jordan College has a roof you are not supposed to be on.
about: Pullman's Oxford is the real one with the Reformation gone the other way: the Church runs the sciences under the name of experimental theology, and the colleges are its rivals. Dæmons settle into a fixed animal form at adolescence, which is the series' most quietly devastating idea — you find out what you are, and then you are it. The alethiometer, a truth-telling instrument read with three needles and a book of symbols, is the plot's engine.

name: Magrathea
blurb: A planet that manufactures other planets to order, currently in recession and asleep for five million years. Ask to see the fjords. They won an award.

name: Meereen
blurb: A pyramid city of coloured brick on a hot bay, mid-revolution and unsure how it feels about that. Fighting pits, harpies, and a queen with dragons.

name: Menzoberranzan
blurb: A drow city carved into stalagmites two miles below the surface, lit by faerie fire, ruled by matriarchs, and organised entirely around murdering your way up the house rankings.
about: The Underdark is a lightless continent under the continent, and Menzoberranzan is its most famous city: eight noble houses in permanent lethal competition, held in check by a goddess who approves of the competition. Salvatore's Drizzt Do'Urden left it, which is the whole point of the character. The architecture — spun stone, glowing sculpture, cathedral-scale caverns — is the most striking thing in the setting.

name: Milliways
blurb: The Restaurant at the End of the Universe, where you dine while the cosmos collapses outside the window, twice nightly. Pay by depositing a penny in your own era.

name: Minas Tirith
blurb: Seven white tiers built into a mountainside, with a view across the Pelennor and a great deal of stairs. Magnificent, ceremonial, and periodically besieged.

name: Mordor
blurb: A volcanic plain of ash and slag under a permanent overcast, ringed by mountains and administered with real commitment. Remarkably quiet in the off-season.

name: Moria
blurb: The greatest dwarf-realm ever delved, now empty except for what moved in afterwards. Astonishing halls. Do not go alone, at night, or at all.

name: Mos Eisley Spaceport
blurb: You will never find a more wretched hive of scum and villainy. Outstanding live music, and the drinks are cheap because the clientele are unlikely to complain.

name: Mustafar
blurb: A world of open lava rivers and mining platforms, where the air is unbreathable and the ground is optional. Historically a poor choice of duelling venue.

name: Naboo
blurb: Lakeside palaces, waterfall cities and rolling green hills, with an entire amphibian civilisation in the planet's core. The most beautiful world in the galaxy and it knows it.

name: Neverland
blurb: An island of pirates, mermaids and lost boys where nobody grows up and the crocodile has swallowed a clock. Endless adventure, and you will forget your parents' faces.

name: New York City
blurb: The real New York, plus a mansion school in Westchester, a sanctum on Bleecker Street, a tower with an A on it, and property damage nobody's insurance covers.
about: Marvel's founding decision was to put superheroes in a real city with real streets rather than an invented Gotham or Metropolis, so that Peter Parker could worry about rent in Queens. The consequence is that Manhattan has been destroyed and rebuilt dozens of times, is under regular alien invasion, and remains the most desirable real estate in fiction. The Sanctum Sanctorum's address, 177A Bleecker Street, is a real corner.

name: Novigrad
blurb: The Continent's biggest free city — docks, banks, brothels, bathhouses and a religious purge in progress. Mages are being burned in the square; business continues.
about: Sapkowski's world is one where the fantastical is being squeezed out by politics, and Novigrad is where you watch it happen: the Eternal Fire's witch hunts are less about theology than about who owns the mage-run banks. Everything is for sale, including the guard. The card game Gwent, invented as flavour, became popular enough to be released as its own product.

name: Oldtown & the Citadel
blurb: The oldest city in Westeros, and the Citadel where maesters forge their chains. The library is the best in the known world, and they will not let you take anything out.

name: Pandora
blurb: A moon of bioluminescent rainforest, floating mountains and a planet-wide neural network. The air will kill you in four minutes and the wildlife will get there first.

name: Qo'noS
blurb: Red skies, volcanic ranges and a culture where dishonour is worse than death and the food is still moving. Superb opera. Bring your own knife.

name: Redwall Abbey
blurb: A red sandstone abbey of mice, moles and hedgehogs in a wood full of woodland, defended by everyone and famous chiefly for the size of its dinners.
about: Jacques wrote the first book to be read aloud to children at a school for the blind, which is why everything is described by taste, sound and texture — the feasts run for pages and have been the subject of actual cookbooks. The abbey is besieged in most books and survives because the peaceful creatures turn out to be extremely willing when pushed. Moles speak in dialect. Badgers do the fighting.

name: Risa
blurb: The Federation's pleasure planet, where the weather is engineered and hospitality is a formal discipline. The statuette means yes. It rains only when someone sabotages the control net.

name: Rivendell
blurb: A hidden house in a river gorge where the food is good, the singing never quite stops and nobody is in any hurry. The finest convalescence in Middle-earth.
photoTopics: Kaitoke Regional Park New Zealand Rivendell

name: Roke Island
blurb: The school of wizardry at the centre of the Archipelago, hidden behind a wind that turns away anyone who should not find it. Nine masters, one Great House, and the Immanent Grove.
about: Le Guin's wizards learn names, not spells — the true name of a thing gives you power over it and responsibility for it, and every act of magic tips the world's balance somewhere else. The Master Namer teaches lists that take years; the Master Patterner lives in a grove of trees that are older than the island and does not teach at all. Ged arrives here as an arrogant boy and lets something out.

name: Salamandastron
blurb: A hollow mountain on the coast, home to the Badger Lord and the Long Patrol hares, who are the finest fighters in the country and by some distance the hungriest.
about: An extinct volcano riddled with tunnels and forges, where badger rulers have been buried in sequence for centuries and sometimes see the future in the fire. The hares of the Long Patrol combine parade-ground manners with appalling violence and an appetite that is a running joke across twenty-two books. It faces the sea, and the trouble usually arrives from it.

name: Selidor
blurb: The last island before the open sea, where the dragons come to die and the land of the dead can be walked into if you are foolish enough to try.
about: Selidor is the westernmost land in Earthsea, and past it there is only water and then the dry stone wall that separates the living from the dead. The Farthest Shore ends here with an old dragon, a dying king and a long walk back that should not be survivable. Le Guin's dead are not tormented — they simply stand about in a grey country with no thirst and no love, which is far worse.

name: Shadar Logoth
blurb: A perfectly preserved dead city that destroyed itself fighting evil by becoming worse. Do not touch anything. Do not stay after dark. Do not let Mashadar touch you.
about: Once Aridhol, it defended itself so ruthlessly that the defence consumed the defenders, and what remains is a hunger with streets. Jordan's cleanest moral: an evil that arises from fighting evil is not thereby better. The city is untouched — furniture, gold, glassware, all sitting there — because everyone who has come to loot it has stayed. Mashadar is a grey mist and it moves.

name: Shadizar
blurb: Shadizar the Wicked, city of thieves and moneylenders, where the temples are richer than the palaces and both are worth robbing. Conan started here, badly.
about: Howard's sin-city archetype: everything is for sale, the priests are running a racket, and the Tower of the Elephant on the hill contains a wizard and something much stranger. Zamora as a whole is a country of ancient, decadent evil, which in pulp means that the architecture is spectacular and the alleys are lethal. Sword and sorcery's template for every thieves' quarter written since.

name: Skellige
blurb: Six storm-battered islands of longships, mead halls and a succession system that involves a lot of shouting. The sea here has things in it that the mainland does not believe in.
about: Norse in every particular except that the sea monsters are real and the druids are politically influential. Clans hold the islands, the king is elected by combat and consensus in roughly that order, and everyone can sail. Sapkowski's Skellige is a small culture that knows it is small; the games rendered it as the most beautiful place in the world and the hardest to survive a winter in.

name: Skyrim
blurb: A cold northern province of pine, snow and mead halls, currently having a civil war, a dragon crisis and an unresolved argument about which god you are allowed to worship.
about: The Nords believe the afterlife is a hall where you fight all day and drink all night, which explains a great deal about their approach to the present one. Every barrow contains a draugr and a shout carved into a wall; every hillside contains a wandering merchant who will tell you they used to be an adventurer. The word-walls and dragon language were invented complete, with a working grammar, and fans sing in it.

name: Solaris Station
blurb: A research station above an ocean that is a single thinking organism. It has read your mind and built something from it, and it is waiting outside your door.

name: Stormwind
blurb: The Alliance's capital: canals, cathedral, a park full of druids and a trade district you will pass through four thousand times. Rebuilt after the orcs razed it, by stonemasons who were never paid.
about: Warcraft's human capital, and the busiest crossroads in the setting — for most of a decade, several hundred thousand people stood in its trade district at once. The unpaid-stonemasons grievance turned the builders into the Defias Brotherhood, which is a rare case of an MMO starting-zone quest chain being about labour relations. The cathedral district's organ music is the most recognisable ambient track in the genre.

name: Stygia
blurb: A black-walled kingdom along a great river, ruled by a priesthood of serpent-worshippers with an interest in what happens to bodies after death, and before it.
about: Howard's Stygia is Egypt with the sun removed and the snakes turned up. Set is worshipped in temples that go further down than up, the sorcerers are the aristocracy, and the whole country is treated by its neighbours as a source of very bad news drifting north. The tone is unmistakably the 1930s pulps' anxiety about the ancient world, and it has furnished every 'evil desert empire' since.

name: Svalbard
blurb: The kingdom of the armoured bears, who forge their own armour from sky-iron and regard it as their soul. There is a palace of ice, a deposed king, and a duel.
about: Pullman's panserbjørne are the best-realised non-humans in modern fantasy precisely because they are not people in fur: they cannot be tricked, except by appealing to the one thing they lack and want. Iorek Byrnison's armour is not clothing, it is the equivalent of a dæmon. The real Svalbard is a Norwegian archipelago you can fly to, with about 2,500 residents and considerably more polar bears than the tourist board mentions.

name: Tar Valon
blurb: A city of ogier-built towers on a river island, home to the White Tower and the only women in the world permitted to channel. Nobody enters a treaty with Tar Valon lightly.
about: The Aes Sedai are bound by three oaths — no lying, no making weapons, no using the One Power to kill except in defence — which makes them the most feared and least trusted people alive, because everyone knows exactly how much room those oaths leave. The Tower is split into seven Ajahs of different colours and purposes, and its politics are the slow, poisonous kind. The buildings were made by Ogier stonemasons and look grown rather than built.
photoTopics: Ile de la Cite Paris aerial

name: Tatooine
blurb: Twin suns, moisture farms and a spaceport bar with a strict no-droids policy. Nothing happens here, which is precisely why so much of it does.
photoTopics: Chott el Djerid Tunisia salt flat

name: The Barrens
blurb: A vast yellow savanna of thorns, zhevras and one very long road, which takes an extremely long time to cross and is famous chiefly for the conversations people had while crossing it.
about: Barrens Chat is a genuine piece of internet folklore: a zone-wide chat channel in which a million players spent 2005 asking each other where Mankrik's wife was. The zone itself is deliberately empty and slow, and the Crossroads is a small outpost that becomes the emotional centre of anyone's first Horde character. Nostalgia for it is entirely disproportionate to its content, which is the point.

name: The Capitol
blurb: A mountain-ringed city of astonishing wealth, cosmetic surgery and televised child murder, whose residents are genuinely puzzled that anyone resents them.
about: Collins built the Capitol out of imperial Rome — the names, the bread and circuses, the tribute system — and dressed it in reality-television gloss. The cruelty is not sadism so much as insulation: its citizens experience the Games as a sporting season and the districts as a supply chain. The food, the fashion and the parties are described in loving, nauseated detail, which is the book's real argument.

name: The Centre of the Earth
blurb: Down a dormant Icelandic volcano to a subterranean ocean lit by electrical discharge, with forests of giant mushrooms and things that should be extinct fighting in the shallows.
photoTopics: Journey to the Centre of the Earth engraving

name: The Citadel
blurb: A vast station of five arms and a central ring, capital of galactic civilisation, built by someone nobody has met. The wards go on for kilometres and the bureaucracy is worse.

name: The Dead Marshes
blurb: A flooded battlefield where the faces of the fallen show under the water. Uniquely atmospheric. Do not follow the lights.

name: The Death Star
blurb: A moon-sized battle station with a superlaser and, famously, a two-metre thermal exhaust port. Immaculate corridors, appalling health and safety, no handrails anywhere.

name: The Emerald City
blurb: A green city at the end of a yellow brick road, ruled by a wizard who turns out to be a balloonist from Omaha. Everyone is very kind and the spectacles are compulsory.
photoTopics: Denslow Wizard of Oz Emerald City

name: The Eyrie
blurb: A castle on a mountain spire reachable only by a mule track and three waystations. Impregnable, spectacular, and the sky cells have no fourth wall.

name: The Forbidden Forest
blurb: Out of bounds to all pupils, which is why so much of every book happens there. Centaurs who read the stars and will not explain, acromantulas who will, and unicorns.
about: The forest is where the school's rules stop, and the series uses it as its consistent boundary between childhood and everything else — the first book's climax, the fifth book's escape, the seventh book's walk to the clearing. The centaurs refuse to intervene in human affairs on principle and resent being asked. Hagrid keeps things in there that he should not.

name: The Forest Moon of Endor
blurb: Thousand-foot redwoods, speeder bikes and a village of small hostile bears who will either eat you or crown you. Beautiful, and much more dangerous than it looks.

name: The Gerudo Desert
blurb: Burning sand by day, freezing by night, and a walled town of warriors who bar men at the gate. The nearest thing Hyrule has to a city with an actual culture.
about: The Gerudo are a nation of women who produce one male child a century, and that child has an unfortunate track record. Gerudo Town enforces its no-men rule strictly enough that the games have made a running joke of the workarounds. The desert around it has sandstorms that disable your map, sinkholes with molduga in them, and a set of ruins that predate the kingdom.

name: The Grey Havens
blurb: A quiet harbour at the end of everything, where white ships leave for the West. A one-way destination, and everyone knows it.

name: The Grizzly Hills
blurb: Autumn forest and log lodges on the edge of a frozen continent, with bears, lumber mills and the single most beloved piece of music anyone has written for a video game zone.
about: Northrend is otherwise an ice continent full of undead, and the Grizzly Hills is the warm exception — permanently in autumn, with woodsmoke and a fiddle-and-flute theme by Russell Brower that people put on to work to fifteen years later. The furbolg have a problem, the worgen have a worse one, and none of that is why anyone remembers the place.

name: The Hundred Acre Wood
blurb: A small wood where the biggest problems are a stuck bear and a lost tail. Nothing bad has ever happened here and nothing bad ever will.
photoTopics: E H Shepard Winnie the Pooh illustration

name: The Imperial City
blurb: A ring of districts around a white tower on an island in a lake, at the exact centre of the continent. The Empire is administered from here, when there is one.
about: The White-Gold Tower was built by elves and taken by men, and the whole imperial project rests on it — which is why every crisis in the series involves something happening to it. The city's Arcane University, Arena and Market District are laid out as a wheel, an idea borrowed from Roman city planning and Dante alike. Cyrodiil is meant to be the boring province, and is: temperate, orderly, and full of paperwork.

name: The Iron Islands
blurb: Wet rock in a cold sea, populated by people who consider farming beneath them and raiding a career. They do not sow. They also do not have much.

name: The Island of Utopia
blurb: Fifty-four identical cities, six-hour working days, gold used for chamber pots, and no private property whatsoever. Immaculately reasonable and quietly unnerving.

name: The Ivory Tower
blurb: A white spiral at the centre of a land made entirely of human imagination, where the Childlike Empress is dying because too few people are still making things up.
about: Fantastica has no borders, because imagination has none, and it is being eaten by the Nothing — a hole that appears wherever people stop believing. The Empress cannot act; she can only wait for a human child to give her a new name. Ende's second half, which the 1984 film omits entirely, is about what happens to someone who can wish for anything: every wish costs a memory, and you can wish yourself into having nothing left to wish with.

name: The Kingdom of Lancre
blurb: A small mountain kingdom you could walk across in a day, mostly vertical, held together by three witches who would strongly prefer you did not need them.
about: Lancre sits on a magical fault line, which is why the local witches — Granny Weatherwax, Nanny Ogg and whoever is currently third — spend most of their time keeping things out rather than letting things in. Witchcraft here is not spells but headology: knowing exactly what people already believe and using it on them. Excellent cheese. Do not accept a drink from Nanny Ogg.

name: The Land of the Houyhnhnms
blurb: A country of rational, virtuous horses who keep degenerate humans as livestock. Deeply peaceful, deeply humbling, and you will not enjoy how you are classified.

name: The Lantern Waste
blurb: A snow-covered wood where a working iron lamp-post stands in the middle of nowhere, marking the place where a wardrobe lets out. Always winter here, until it isn't.
about: The lamp-post grew from a fragment of London street furniture dropped into new-made soil at the creation of the world, which is the sort of joke Lewis enjoyed. This is the first Narnia anyone sees, and for a hundred years it was held under the White Witch's permanent winter with no Christmas. The thaw, when it comes, is described more vividly than any battle in the series.

name: The Misty Mountains
blurb: A thousand-mile spine of snow, storm and things living under it. The passes are worse than they look, and they look bad.
photoTopics: Southern Alps New Zealand snow peaks

name: The Mushroom Kingdom
blurb: Cheerful hills, floating brick blocks, warp pipes to everywhere and physics that reward jumping. The princess is in another castle, but the castle is very nice.
about: There is no consistent map, no real history and no explanation for the pipes, and none of that has ever mattered — the kingdom exists to be moved through, and its geography is designed around the arc of a jump. Miyamoto's rule was that the first eight seconds should teach you everything; those eight seconds are World 1-1, which is probably the most studied level design in the world.
photoTopics: Rolling green hills blue sky clouds

name: The Nine Circles
blurb: A descending funnel of nine circles, each with a punishment precisely fitted to its sin, ending in a frozen lake rather than fire. Abandon all hope, etc.

name: The Ringworld
blurb: A band of engineered land circling a star, with three million times Earth's surface area and a civilisation that has forgotten how any of it works.

name: The Shattered Plains
blurb: A thousand square miles of plateaus separated by chasms, scoured every few days by storms that would strip the skin off you. The war fought across it has lasted six years and achieved nothing.
about: Roshar's ecology is built around the highstorms: the plants retract into shells, the animals are crustaceans, and there is no grass that does not hide. The plateaus are the shattered remains of something, and the chasms between them are full of bones, gemhearts and one very large predator. Sanderson wrote the bridge crews — men used as expendable equipment — as the emotional engine of the first book.

name: The Shire
blurb: Rolling green farmland, six meals a day and a deep suspicion of anything that happens. The single most restful destination in fiction, provided nobody knocks on your door about a quest.
photoTopics: Waikato rolling green farmland New Zealand

name: The Smoking Sea & Valyria
blurb: The greatest empire that ever lived, destroyed in a single day and still burning four hundred years later. Nobody who sails in comes back healthy.

name: The Two Rivers
blurb: Sheep, tabac and the best wool in the world, in a corner of the map so quiet that its people have forgotten they were once the last soldiers of a fallen nation.
about: Jordan's deliberate echo of the Shire: an ordinary farming district whose ordinariness is the whole point, and out of which walk three of the most consequential people in the world. The Women's Circle and the Village Council disagree about everything and run the place perfectly well. It is also, quietly, the remnant of Manetheren, a kingdom that died refusing to surrender — which becomes relevant.

name: The Wall
blurb: Seven hundred feet of ice running three hundred miles, manned by an order of convicts and younger sons. The view from the top is unmatched and the posting is for life.

name: The Wine-Dark Sea
blurb: Island-hop between a cyclops, a witch who turns men into pigs, sirens, and a whirlpool. Ten years is the standard itinerary. Hospitality is sacred, and so is revenge.

name: Trantor
blurb: Forty billion people under a continuous metal dome covering the whole planet, and the Imperial Library where a mathematician worked out exactly how it all ends.

name: Überwald
blurb: Dark forests, castles on crags and a vampire aristocracy going through a difficult modernisation. The werewolves are the reasonable ones. Mind the dwarf mines.
about: Every Central European gothic cliché, gathered in one place and then quietly interrogated. The vampires have formed a temperance league and wear black ribbons; the werewolves have a monarchy; the dwarfs are having an argument about whether female dwarfs are allowed to admit they exist. Pratchett's point is always that the monsters are managing, and the trouble comes from anyone insisting they go back to being monsters.

name: Unseen University
blurb: The Discworld's premier college of magic, whose faculty long ago worked out that the surest way to avoid magical catastrophe is an enormous lunch. The Library is not shelved in three dimensions.
about: Wizards here are not adventurers; they are academics with very large hats and a serious interest in the dinner rota. The Librarian was turned into an orangutan and declined to be turned back, since it improved his reach. L-space — the principle that all libraries are connected because sufficient books warp reality — is the university's one genuinely dangerous idea, and it is guarded by an ape with a banana.

name: Urithiru
blurb: A tower city of a hundred levels carved into a mountain above the storms, with a garden at the top that grows without soil and a lift system nobody has repaired in millennia.
about: Abandoned for four thousand years and rediscovered by people with no manual. Urithiru sits above the highstorms — the only place on Roshar that does — and is connected to every other Radiant city by a network of portals in its basement. Sanderson's worldbuilding runs on rules: the tower has a mind, the mind has been asleep, and waking it turns out to have consequences that are entirely foreshadowed.

name: Volantis
blurb: The oldest daughter of Valyria, split by the Rhoyne and the Long Bridge, hot enough that the elephants move slowly. Five slaves to every free man, and a red temple that never sleeps.

name: Vulcan
blurb: A hot, thin-aired desert world of monasteries and forge-red rock, populated by people who suppressed their emotions and have been quietly smug about it for two thousand years.

name: Vvardenfell
blurb: An ash-covered volcanic island of giant mushroom towers, insect transport and three living gods with a public relations problem. Nothing here looks like anywhere else.
about: The most deliberately alien setting in mainstream fantasy: the houses are grown from fungus or carved from beetle shells, the taxi service is a giant flea, and the state religion is run by three people who made themselves divine and are now watching it wear off. The ash storms are genuinely dangerous and the local disease will turn you into something. Bethesda has never made anything this strange again.

name: Wakanda
blurb: A nation that hid itself for centuries behind a projection of farmland while building the most advanced city on Earth on top of the world's only vibranium deposit.
about: Created by Lee and Kirby in 1966 as a direct rebuttal to how Africa was drawn in comics, and rebuilt by Ta-Nehisi Coates and the 2018 film into something with a working political argument: what a country owes the world when it has never been colonised and could help. The tribal council, the Dora Milaje and the herb-granted throne are all bound up in the succession, which is settled by ritual combat at a waterfall.

name: Waterdeep
blurb: The City of Splendours: a huge, wealthy port run by masked Lords nobody can identify, sitting on top of the largest dungeon in the world.
about: Waterdeep is where every Forgotten Realms campaign starts, because it has a guild for everything, a tavern for every kind of trouble and Undermountain directly beneath it — a dungeon of more than twenty levels built by a mad wizard who is still down there and still redecorating. The Lords wear enchanted masks in public so that assassinating them achieves nothing. Baldur's Gate is a few weeks' ride south and considerably less pleasant.

name: Winterfell
blurb: A granite castle built over hot springs, so the walls stay warm while everything outside freezes. Excellent hosts, if you survive the feast.

name: Wonderland
blurb: A croquet ground with flamingos, a permanent tea party, and a queen with strong views on beheading. Nothing here follows from anything else and everyone finds you rude.
photoTopics: Alice in Wonderland Tenniel Cheshire Cat
Alice down the rabbit hole illustration

name: Yavin 4
blurb: A jungle moon of a gas giant, with Massassi temples rising above the canopy. Humid, loud with insects, and historically good for hiding a fleet.
